title: Inflammatory Musculoskeletal Diseases
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the inflammatory, crystal, and overuse disorders of joints, entheses, bursae, tendons, and muscle: the HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, gout and pseudogout, the inflammatory myopathies, polymyalgia rheumatica, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, fibromyalgia, and the common soft tissue lesions. Board questions usually turn on a small number of discriminating findings: which joints are involved, whether the enthesis or the synovium is the target, crystal shape and birefringence, whether CK and strength are abnormal, and which infection or metabolic state came first. If you can explain the tissue being attacked and why, each pattern of findings follows.

connections.to: Rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis (MS-13 joint chapters)
connections.how: Spondyloarthropathies and crystal arthritis are defined largely by how they differ from erosive synovial RA and degenerative OA.
HLA-B27, the IL-23 and IL-17 axis, complement-mediated vascular injury, and the NLRP3 inflammasome explain the main diseases here.
Serum urate depends on purine turnover, HGPRT salvage, and proximal tubular urate transport.
Aortitis with aortic regurgitation, giant cell arteritis, and restrictive or interstitial lung disease are the main extra-articular threats.
Chlamydia and enteric pathogens trigger reactive arthritis, and Staphylococcus aureus causes septic bursitis.

sections.title: Ankylosing spondylitis: enthesitis, sacroiliitis, and spinal fusion

blocks.text: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the prototype seronegative spondyloarthropathy: a chronic inflammatory disease of the axial skeleton that begins at the sacroiliac joints and the entheses of the spine. About 90% of patients of European descent carry HLA-B27, an MHC class I allele, yet only a small fraction of B27 carriers ever develop AS, so the gene confers susceptibility rather than disease. Onset is usually in the late teens to the 30s, and men are affected about two to three times as often as women and tend to have more severe radiographic progression.

The exact role of HLA-B27 is unsettled. Leading explanations are presentation of arthritogenic microbial or self peptides to CD8 T cells, misfolding of the B27 heavy chain that triggers an unfolded protein response, and abnormal B27 heavy chain dimers recognized by innate receptors. These converge on the IL-23 and IL-17 axis and on TNF, which drive inflammation at entheses, where mechanical stress concentrates.

The key distinction from rheumatoid arthritis is what follows inflammation. In RA, pannus erodes bone and the joint is destroyed with periarticular bone loss. In AS, an early erosive phase at the enthesis is followed by repair that overshoots: fibrous tissue replaces the inflamed attachment and then ossifies. At the vertebral corners this produces syndesmophytes, thin vertical bridges that grow from the outer annulus fibrosus to the next vertebra. When many levels fuse, the radiograph shows a bamboo spine, and the sacroiliac joints become eroded, sclerotic, and finally fused, usually bilaterally.

blocks.text: Inflammatory back pain explains itself through this biology. Pain and stiffness arise from inflamed entheses that stiffen with rest and loosen with movement, so symptoms are worst in the morning and in the second half of the night, last more than 30 minutes on rising, and improve with exercise but not with rest. Mechanical back pain behaves the opposite way. As the costovertebral and costotransverse joints are involved, chest expansion falls (under about 2.5 cm at the fourth intercostal space), and lumbar flexion is lost, measured by the modified Schober test. Advanced disease produces loss of lumbar lordosis and fixed thoracic kyphosis. Hips and shoulders are the joints outside the spine most often involved.

blocks.title: Inflammatory versus mechanical back pain
rows: ESR and CRP may be raised
blocks.caption: Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are negative in AS, which is the meaning of seronegative.

blocks.text: The inflammation of AS is not confined to the spine. Sites outside the skeleton that share fibrous attachments, collagen-rich walls, or the same immune milieu are also involved.

Acute anterior uveitis (iritis) is the most common extra-articular feature, occurring in about a third of patients over their lifetime. It is typically unilateral, recurrent, and may alternate between eyes, presenting with a painful red eye, photophobia, and blurred vision. Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body releases cells and protein into the anterior chamber; untreated attacks can leave posterior synechiae (adhesions of iris to lens), cataract, or glaucoma. Painful acute uveitis in AS contrasts with the painless chronic uveitis of oligoarticular JIA (C14).

Aortitis affects the aortic root. Inflammation centered on the adventitia and vasa vasorum causes intimal proliferation and fibrosis that dilates the root and thickens and shortens the aortic cusps, so the valve fails to coapt and aortic regurgitation results: a diastolic decrescendo murmur and wide pulse pressure. Fibrosis can extend below the valve into the membranous septum and the base of the anterior mitral leaflet, injuring the AV node or His bundle and producing heart block.

Lung function becomes restrictive mainly from the chest wall. Fusion of the costovertebral joints and thoracic kyphosis fix the rib cage, so vital capacity and total lung capacity fall while the FEV1 to FVC ratio stays normal or high and diffusing capacity is preserved; the diaphragm takes over most ventilation. A smaller number develop apical fibrobullous disease of the upper lobes.

Finally, the fused spine is both rigid and osteoporotic, because inflammation and immobility reduce bone mass inside the vertebral bodies even as bone forms at their margins. A rigid column behaves like a long bone, so minor trauma such as a fall from standing can fracture it, most often in the lower cervical spine. These fractures pass through the whole fused segment, are unstable, and carry a high risk of spinal cord injury. Chronic inflammation can also cause secondary (AA) amyloidosis.

blocks.caption: Each complication follows from the tissue involved.

blocks.predict: A 45-year-old man with long-standing AS falls from standing and has neck pain but a normal neurological examination. Why should this be treated as a possible unstable fracture?
blocks.explain: The fused, osteoporotic spine acts as a single rigid lever. Force that a mobile spine would absorb across many discs concentrates at one level and fractures through the entire column, often in the lower cervical spine, so the fracture is unstable and the cord can be injured later.
blocks.check: The paragraph on vertebral fractures and the bone changes in C01.

blocks.text: A bursa is a closed sac lined by synovium-like cells and containing a thin film of fluid that lets tendon, muscle, or skin glide over bone. Bursae are either subcutaneous (between skin and a bony prominence, such as the prepatellar and olecranon bursae) or deep (beneath tendons, such as the subacromial and trochanteric bursae). Bursitis is inflammation of this lining, which then secretes excess fluid and swells. The location of a bursa predicts its cause: superficial bursae suffer pressure and skin breaks, and deep bursae suffer friction from overused tendons.

Repeated pressure or friction produces aseptic bursitis. Prepatellar bursitis follows prolonged kneeling and gives a fluctuant swelling in front of the patella with a preserved knee range of motion, because the joint itself is not involved. Olecranon bursitis follows leaning on the elbow, direct trauma, or gout and rheumatoid arthritis, and presents as a soft swelling over the tip of the elbow. Subacromial (subdeltoid) bursitis accompanies supraspinatus impingement under the acromion (C11). Trochanteric bursitis causes lateral hip pain worse when lying on that side or climbing stairs, often together with gluteus medius and minimus tendinopathy.

Septic bursitis almost always involves the superficial prepatellar or olecranon bursae, because a small skin break lets organisms in directly. Staphylococcus aureus causes most cases, followed by streptococci. The bursa is warm, red, and very tender, often with cellulitis around it, and fever may be absent. Aspirated fluid separates the causes: septic fluid has a high white cell count with neutrophils and organisms on Gram stain or culture, gouty bursitis shows urate crystals, and traumatic bursitis is often bloody.

sections.title: Fibromyalgia: a disorder of central pain processing

blocks.text: Fibromyalgia is chronic widespread pain without damage or inflammation in the painful tissues. The abnormality lies in how the nervous system processes pain. It affects about 2 to 4% of adults, more often women, and usually begins in middle adulthood. Because the muscles and joints are structurally normal, ESR, CRP, CK, and muscle biopsy are normal, and the absence of objective inflammation is part of the picture rather than evidence against it.

The mechanism is central sensitization. Repeated input to dorsal horn neurons raises their excitability through glutamate acting on NMDA receptors (the basis of temporal summation, or wind-up), so the same stimulus produces a growing response. Descending inhibitory pathways from the brainstem, which use serotonin and norepinephrine to damp dorsal horn transmission, are less effective. Cerebrospinal fluid substance P is raised, and functional imaging shows that a given pressure activates pain-processing regions at lower intensity than in controls. The results are allodynia, in which light touch or pressure hurts, and hyperalgesia, in which painful stimuli hurt more than they should.

blocks.title: Self-sustaining loop of central sensitization
steps: Ongoing input or stress activates dorsal horn neurons
Glutamate and NMDA receptors raise neuronal excitability
Descending serotonin and norepinephrine inhibition is weak
Normal input is felt as widespread pain

Poor sleep and stress lower pain thresholds further
blocks.caption: Sleep disturbance and pain reinforce each other, which is why both are central to the diagnosis.

blocks.text: Clinically, pain is widespread (both sides of the body, above and below the waist, and axial), present for at least 3 months, and accompanied by fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive difficulty often called fibro fog. Many patients also have irritable bowel syndrome, migraine or tension headache, temporomandibular disorder, depression, or anxiety, conditions that share altered central processing. Older criteria required tenderness at 11 of 18 tender points; current criteria score the extent of pain and the severity of symptoms instead.

The diagnostic reasoning relies on what is normal. Strength is normal, distinguishing it from myositis. CK is normal, excluding muscle necrosis. ESR and CRP are normal, separating it from polymyalgia rheumatica, which has girdle-limited pain in older adults with high inflammatory markers. Hypothyroidism, which can cause diffuse aches and fatigue, is excluded with thyroid function tests.

Uric acid is the end product of purine degradation in humans, because humans lack uricase, the enzyme that converts urate to the far more soluble allantoin in most other mammals. At physiological pH, uric acid exists mostly as the urate anion, which saturates plasma as monosodium urate at about 6.8 mg/dL (about 400 micromol/L) at 37°C (98.6°F). Above this level, called hyperuricemia, crystals can form, and solubility falls further in cooler tissue such as the toes.

blocks.title: Purine degradation to uric acid
steps: AMP is deaminated to IMP, then inosine
Inosine becomes hypoxanthine
GMP becomes guanosine, then guanine
Guanine is deaminated to xanthine
Xanthine oxidase: hypoxanthine to xanthine
Xanthine oxidase: xanthine to uric acid
blocks.caption: Xanthine oxidase catalyzes both final steps. HGPRT normally salvages hypoxanthine and guanine back to IMP and GMP before they are degraded.

blocks.text: Serum urate reflects a balance between production and excretion. About two thirds of daily urate is excreted by the kidney and one third by the gut. Urate is freely filtered, then mostly reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by URAT1 and GLUT9 while a smaller amount is secreted by organic anion transporters, leaving fractional excretion near 10%. URAT1 exchanges filtered urate for organic anions from inside the cell, so anything that loads those anions increases urate reabsorption, and volume contraction raises proximal reabsorption generally.

Underexcretion causes about 90% of gout. Chronic kidney disease lowers filtration. Thiazide and loop diuretics cause volume contraction that enhances proximal reabsorption and compete with urate for tubular secretion. Lactate from alcohol and ketoacids from fasting are exchanged for urate through URAT1, and low-dose aspirin reduces urate secretion. Lead nephropathy and cyclosporine also reduce excretion.

Overproduction accounts for the rest. In tumor lysis, the nucleic acids of dying cells are degraded to urate, and high cell turnover in myeloproliferative disorders and severe psoriasis does the same more slowly. In Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT), the salvage of hypoxanthine and guanine fails, so they are degraded instead, and the PRPP they would have consumed accumulates and stimulates PRPP amidotransferase, the committed step of de novo purine synthesis. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke disease) raises urate both by overproduction and by underexcretion.

blocks.title: Causes of hyperuricemia
rows: Volume contraction increases proximal reabsorption; compete for secretion
Lactate and ketoacids exchanged for urate via URAT1
Degradation of nucleic acids from dying cells
Salvage fails; excess PRPP drives de novo synthesis
PRPP excess, ATP breakdown, lactate competing for excretion
blocks.caption: Underexcretion is far more common than overproduction.

blocks.title: Why glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency raises urate in three ways
blocks.text: Without glucose-6-phosphatase, the liver cannot release free glucose, so glucose-6-phosphate accumulates. First, excess glucose-6-phosphate enters the pentose phosphate pathway, producing ribose-5-phosphate and therefore PRPP, which drives de novo purine synthesis. Second, phosphate trapped in sugar phosphates lowers free hepatic phosphate, so ATP cannot be regenerated; ADP and AMP accumulate and AMP is degraded through IMP and hypoxanthine to urate. Third, fasting hypoglycemia drives lactic acidosis, and lactate is exchanged for urate in the proximal tubule, reducing excretion. Two routes increase production and one reduces excretion.

sections.title: Gout: clinical, crystal, and radiographic findings

blocks.text: Most people with hyperuricemia never develop gout; crystals must form in a joint and be recognized by the innate immune system. Gout typically progresses from asymptomatic hyperuricemia, through acute attacks separated by symptom-free intercritical periods, to chronic tophaceous gout. It affects men after puberty and women mainly after menopause, because estrogen increases renal urate excretion.

An acute attack follows a rise, or any abrupt change, in serum urate that causes crystals to form or to shed from deposits on cartilage. Alcohol (especially beer, which also contains purines), meals rich in organ meat or shellfish, dehydration, surgery, and acute illness are typical triggers. Serum urate may be normal during the attack itself, so a normal level does not exclude gout. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is the site of about half of first attacks (podagra), because it is cool and repeatedly stressed, both of which favor crystal formation. The attack starts suddenly, often overnight, and the joint becomes hot, red, swollen, and too painful to touch, peaking within a day.

blocks.title: How urate crystals cause an acute attack
steps: Urate crystals form or shed into the joint
Macrophages phagocytose crystals
NLRP3 inflammasome activates caspase-1
Caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1 beta to active IL-1 beta
Endothelial activation recruits neutrophils
Neutrophils release mediators: hot, red, swollen joint
blocks.caption: Gout is an autoinflammatory response driven by the innate immune system, not by autoantibodies.

blocks.text: Synovial fluid analysis is definitive. Urate crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent under compensated polarized light: they appear yellow when their long axis lies parallel to the slow axis of the compensator and blue when perpendicular. The fluid is inflammatory, with white cell counts commonly between about 2,000 and 100,000 per microliter, mostly neutrophils that often contain crystals.

Chronic disease produces tophi: chalky deposits of urate surrounded by macrophages and foreign body giant cells, a granulomatous reaction, in the helix of the ear, olecranon bursa, Achilles tendon, and around finger joints. Urate dissolves in water-based formalin, so tissue for crystal identification is fixed in alcohol. Tophi in bone produce punched-out erosions with sclerotic borders and overhanging edges, while joint space is preserved until late, unlike RA. In the kidney, uric acid stones form because uric acid (pKa about 5.5) is poorly soluble in acidic urine; they are radiolucent on plain film. Urate deposits in the medullary interstitium cause chronic urate nephropathy, and massive urate release in tumor lysis precipitates in tubules and causes acute kidney injury.

blocks.caption: Each finding follows from urate chemistry or the tissue reaction to crystals.

blocks.text: The idiopathic inflammatory myopathies share symmetric proximal muscle weakness, raised CK, and myofiber necrosis, but they differ in what the immune system attacks. Weakness of the shoulder and hip girdles shows up as difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, or lifting the arms to comb hair. Involvement of the striated muscle of the pharynx and upper esophagus causes dysphagia and aspiration, and myocarditis can occur. Distal strength, sensation, and reflexes are preserved early, which separates myopathy from neuropathy.

Dermatomyositis is a vasculopathy. Type I interferon signaling and deposition of the complement membrane attack complex (C5b-9) injure endomysial capillaries, which drop out. The fibers at the periphery of each fascicle sit at the watershed of the remaining blood supply, so they become ischemic and atrophic, producing perifascicular atrophy. Inflammatory cells, mainly CD4 T cells, B cells, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, gather around vessels and in the perimysium rather than invading fibers. The same vascular injury affects skin: a heliotrope rash (violet discoloration of the upper eyelids, often with periorbital edema), Gottron papules (violaceous scaly papules over the knuckles), and photodistributed erythema of the upper chest (V sign) and upper back (shawl sign). Dermatomyositis also occurs in children, often with calcinosis.

In adults, dermatomyositis is associated with internal cancer, most often ovarian, lung, gastrointestinal, and pancreatic carcinoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma in Southeast Asian populations. Risk is highest around the time of diagnosis, consistent with a paraneoplastic immune response to antigens shared by tumor and regenerating muscle. Antibodies to TIF1-gamma mark the highest risk.

Polymyositis is a direct cytotoxic attack. Muscle fibers abnormally express MHC class I, and CD8 T cells in the endomysium surround and invade non-necrotic fibers and kill them with perforin and granzymes. There is no rash, and the cancer association is weaker. Polymyositis is now diagnosed less often, because many cases once given this name turn out to be inclusion body myositis or necrotizing myopathy.

Antibodies to aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, of which anti-Jo-1 (anti-histidyl tRNA synthetase) is the most common, define the antisynthetase syndrome in either disease: myositis with interstitial lung disease, Raynaud phenomenon, nonerosive arthritis, fever, and mechanic's hands (cracked, hyperkeratotic skin on the radial fingers). Interstitial lung disease is a leading cause of death in these patients.

sections.title: Biopsy and laboratory findings that separate myositis, polymyalgia rheumatica, and steroid myopathy

blocks.text: Patients with inflammatory myositis, polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), and glucocorticoid (steroid) myopathy all complain of trouble with the shoulders and hips, so the work-up must separate true weakness from pain-limited movement, and muscle destruction from muscle atrophy. Three questions do most of the work: Is strength actually reduced? Is CK raised? Is there inflammation in the muscle?

CK is a cytoplasmic enzyme of skeletal muscle that leaks into blood only when the sarcolemma is breached. In inflammatory myositis, fibers are necrotic, so CK is raised, often to 10 or more times the upper limit of normal, along with aldolase, AST, ALT, and LDH. Electromyography shows a myopathic pattern with spontaneous fibrillation from irritable fibers, and MRI shows muscle edema that can guide biopsy. Biopsy shows inflammatory infiltrates, necrotic and regenerating fibers, and the pattern specific to the subtype (C07). CK can be normal in dermatomyositis limited to the skin or when muscle is already atrophic late in disease.

In PMR, the inflammation is in bursae, tendon sheaths, and synovium around the girdle joints, not in muscle (C09). Strength is normal when pain is accounted for, CK is normal, muscle biopsy is normal, and ESR and CRP are high.

Glucocorticoids cause a myopathy by catabolism rather than inflammation. They reduce muscle protein synthesis by inhibiting IGF-1 and mTOR signaling and increase protein breakdown through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Fast glycolytic type II fibers are most affected. The result is painless proximal weakness, worse in the legs, with normal CK because fibers shrink rather than die, and a biopsy showing type II fiber atrophy without inflammation or necrosis. Endogenous excess in Cushing syndrome does the same.

blocks.title: Separating the three disorders
rows: Type II fiber atrophy, no inflammation
blocks.caption: High CK means fibers are dying; normal CK with weakness points to atrophy, and normal CK with normal strength points away from muscle.

blocks.title: A myositis patient who gets weaker on glucocorticoids
blocks.text: A woman with polymyositis improved over two months on high-dose prednisone, and her CK fell from about 30 times normal to normal. Now her hip weakness is worse and she cannot rise from a chair, yet she has no muscle pain. Two explanations compete: a relapse of myositis or steroid myopathy. A relapse would destroy fibers again, so CK would rise and MRI would show new muscle edema. Her CK is still normal and there is no edema, which fits fiber atrophy without necrosis. The most likely cause is steroid myopathy; a biopsy, if done, would show type II fiber atrophy without inflammatory infiltrates.

sections.title: Polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis

blocks.text: Polymyalgia rheumatica is an inflammatory disorder of adults over 50, most often in their 70s, women about twice as often as men, and most common in people of northern European descent. It presents with bilateral aching and stiffness of the shoulders, neck, and hip girdle, worst in the morning and after rest, often lasting more than 45 minutes. Patients struggle to turn over in bed, get up, or raise their arms. Fatigue, low-grade fever, weight loss, and malaise reflect systemic inflammation.

Despite the name, the muscle itself is not inflamed. Ultrasound and MRI show subacromial and subdeltoid bursitis, biceps tenosynovitis, glenohumeral synovitis, and trochanteric bursitis. That explains the laboratory picture: ESR is typically above 40 mm/h and CRP and IL-6 are raised, often with a normocytic anemia of inflammation, but CK and muscle biopsy are normal. Strength is normal when pain is controlled, which is the key difference from myositis (C08).

PMR and giant cell arteritis (GCA) are best viewed as parts of one disease spectrum. About 15 to 20% of people with PMR have GCA, and about 40 to 50% of people with GCA have PMR symptoms. GCA is a granulomatous vasculitis of large and medium arteries, especially branches of the external carotid such as the superficial temporal artery, plus the ophthalmic artery and the aorta. Dendritic cells in the adventitia activate CD4 T cells that produce IFN-gamma (Th1) and IL-17 (Th17); macrophages and multinucleated giant cells fragment the internal elastic lamina, and the intima thickens until the lumen narrows. The patchy distribution (skip lesions) means a short biopsy can be falsely negative.

blocks.text: Symptoms of GCA follow from narrowed arteries: new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication from ischemic masseters during chewing, and visual disturbance. Large vessel disease can cause arm claudication, unequal arm blood pressures, and late thoracic aortic aneurysm. In a patient with PMR, any of these symptoms means GCA must be considered urgently.

blocks.predict: A 72-year-old with shoulder and hip stiffness, ESR 85 mm/h, and normal CK develops pain in the jaw when chewing. What has changed, and what is at risk?
blocks.explain: Jaw claudication means the masseter is ischemic during use, which points to giant cell arteritis narrowing branches of the external carotid. The same process in the posterior ciliary arteries can infarct the optic nerve head and cause permanent vision loss.

blocks.text: Reactive arthritis is a sterile inflammatory arthritis that appears about 1 to 4 weeks after an infection elsewhere in the body. The triggers are genitourinary infection with Chlamydia trachomatis or enteric infection with Shigella (especially S. flexneri), Salmonella, Yersinia, or Campylobacter jejuni. It is a spondyloarthropathy: it targets entheses, joints of the lower limb, the eye, and mucous membranes, and it is associated with HLA-B27, which also predicts more severe and chronic disease, although many patients are B27 negative.

The joint is sterile, so synovial fluid cultures are negative, but it is not free of bacterial material. Chlamydia can persist in synovium in a viable but nonculturable form, and enteric bacteria deliver lipopolysaccharide and other antigens to the joint inside phagocytes. A T cell response to these persisting antigens, shaped by HLA-B27 and possibly by molecular mimicry between bacterial and self peptides, drives inflammation. This is why the arthritis follows the infection rather than accompanying it, and why culture of the joint fails.

The classic triad is arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis, although all three occur together in only a minority. The arthritis is an asymmetric oligoarthritis of large weight-bearing joints such as the knees and ankles, often with dactylitis and enthesitis at the Achilles tendon and plantar fascia, and sometimes asymmetric sacroiliitis. Conjunctivitis is usually early and sterile; anterior uveitis can occur later. Urethritis or cervicitis can be sterile and can follow an enteric trigger. Mucocutaneous lesions include keratoderma blennorrhagicum, hyperkeratotic pustular plaques on the soles and palms that resemble pustular psoriasis histologically, circinate balanitis, and painless oral ulcers. Most episodes resolve within about 3 to 12 months, but a proportion become recurrent or chronic.

blocks.title: Reactive arthritis compared with disseminated gonococcal infection
rows: Keratoderma blennorrhagicum on soles and palms
blocks.caption: Both follow a sexually transmitted infection, but only gonococcal arthritis contains live organisms in the joint.

sections.title: Tendinopathy: tendinosis, epicondylitis, and supraspinatus impingement

blocks.text: A tendon is made of tightly packed, parallel type I collagen fibrils produced by sparse tenocytes, with little ground substance and a poor blood supply. This structure resists tension well but heals slowly. Tendinopathy is the general term for pain and impaired function in an overused tendon. Despite the old label tendinitis, chronic tendinopathy is mainly degenerative and is better called tendinosis.

Repeated loading creates microtears faster than tenocytes can repair them. The failed healing response leaves disorganized, thinner collagen with more type III collagen, increased proteoglycan and water (mucoid degeneration), rounded and abnormal tenocytes, and ingrowth of small vessels accompanied by nerve fibers. Inflammatory cells are scarce in established disease. The new nerve fibers and local mediators such as glutamate and substance P likely explain the pain, and the weakened matrix explains the risk of rupture.

Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) affects the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle, mainly the extensor carpi radialis brevis. Repetitive gripping and wrist extension load this origin, so pain is reproduced by resisted wrist extension and by gripping. Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) affects the common flexor-pronator origin on the medial epicondyle, mainly pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis, and pain is reproduced by resisted wrist flexion and forearm pronation; the ulnar nerve lies just behind the medial epicondyle and can be irritated.

Supraspinatus impingement is explained by anatomy. The supraspinatus tendon passes through the subacromial space, between the humeral head and the coracoacromial arch (acromion, coracoacromial ligament, and coracoid process), with the subacromial bursa above it. Near its insertion on the greater tubercle is a relatively hypovascular zone. During abduction from about 60 to 120 degrees, the greater tubercle and tendon pass under the arch and are compressed, producing a painful arc; below and above that range the tendon is clear of the arch. Overhead activity, a hooked acromion, and acromioclavicular osteophytes narrow the space. Chronic impingement can progress to a rotator cuff tear, which weakens active abduction while passive motion remains full.

blocks.title: Tendinopathies of the elbow and shoulder
blocks.caption: Pain arises where the loaded tendon attaches to bone or passes under a bony arch.

sections.title: De Quervain tenosynovitis, plantar fasciitis, and Achilles tendinopathy

blocks.text: De Quervain tenosynovitis affects the first dorsal compartment of the wrist, where the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons share a fibro-osseous tunnel over the radial styloid. Repetitive thumb abduction and wrist ulnar deviation, typical of lifting an infant, cause the retinaculum and tendon sheath to thicken, narrowing the tunnel so the tendons glide painfully. Histology shows thickening and myxoid change more than acute inflammation. It is most common in women aged 30 to 50 and in late pregnancy and the postpartum period. Pain and tenderness lie over the radial styloid, and the Finkelstein test, with the thumb flexed into the palm and the wrist deviated toward the ulna, stretches both tendons through the narrowed compartment and reproduces the pain.

Plantar fasciitis is degeneration of the plantar fascia (aponeurosis) at its origin on the medial tubercle of the calcaneus. The fascia supports the longitudinal arch, and dorsiflexion of the toes during push-off winds it tight (the windlass mechanism), so repetitive loading stresses its origin. Overnight the foot rests in plantar flexion and the fascia shortens, so the first steps in the morning stretch it suddenly and cause sharp medial heel pain that eases as the tissue warms up. Risk factors include obesity, prolonged standing, running, flat or high arches, and a tight Achilles tendon that limits ankle dorsiflexion. A calcaneal spur is often present but is an association, not the cause.

Achilles tendinopathy most often affects the midportion of the tendon, about 2 to 6 cm above its insertion, where blood supply is poorest, causing pain and fusiform thickening; insertional disease occurs at the calcaneus. Rupture produces a sudden pop, as if kicked in the heel, with a palpable gap and loss of plantar flexion when the calf is squeezed (Thompson test). Fluoroquinolones raise the risk of tendinopathy and rupture. They are toxic to tenocytes, increase matrix metalloproteinase activity, generate oxidative stress, and reduce collagen synthesis. Risk is higher over age 60, with concurrent systemic glucocorticoids, with kidney disease, and after organ transplantation, and it can appear within days of exposure and in both tendons. Achilles enthesitis is also a feature of the spondyloarthropathies (C10).

blocks.text: Psoriatic arthritis develops in roughly a quarter to a third of people with psoriasis. Skin disease usually comes first, but in about 15% the arthritis appears before the rash, so the nails, scalp, umbilicus, and gluteal cleft should be examined in any unexplained inflammatory arthritis. Like the other spondyloarthropathies, it is seronegative and centers on the enthesis, and it shares the IL-23 and IL-17 pathway with psoriatic skin. HLA-Cw6 is linked mainly to the skin disease, whereas HLA-B27 is linked to axial (spinal and sacroiliac) involvement.

The distinctive features follow from enthesitis. The distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint lies next to the nail, and the extensor tendon enthesis at the DIP joint is anatomically continuous with the nail bed. Inflammation of this nail and enthesis unit explains why DIP arthritis travels with nail pitting and onycholysis. Dactylitis, a sausage-shaped digit, arises when flexor tenosynovitis, synovitis, and soft tissue edema involve the whole finger or toe at once. Patterns vary: DIP-predominant arthritis, asymmetric oligoarthritis, symmetric polyarthritis that resembles RA, axial disease, and the rare destructive arthritis mutilans.

Radiographs show both erosion and new bone, the combination that marks spondyloarthropathy. Erosion of the head of a phalanx tapers it to a point, which sits in a widened, cupped base of the adjacent phalanx, the pencil-in-cup deformity. Fluffy periosteal new bone forms next to the joint, and periarticular bone density is usually preserved. Rheumatoid arthritis, by contrast, is a symmetric synovitis of the MCP, PIP, and wrist joints that spares the DIP joints, is associated with HLA-DR4 and with rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies, and produces marginal erosions with periarticular osteopenia and no new bone.

blocks.predict: A patient has swelling of the DIP joints of two fingers, pitting of those nails, and no rash. Why does nail pitting make psoriatic arthritis more likely than osteoarthritis or RA?
blocks.explain: The DIP extensor enthesis is continuous with the nail bed, so enthesitis at the DIP joint also disturbs the nail matrix. RA spares the DIP joint, and the Heberden nodes of osteoarthritis are bony enlargements without nail disease.

blocks.text: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is arthritis that begins before the 16th birthday, lasts at least 6 weeks, and has no other identified cause such as infection, malignancy, or trauma. It is a group of diseases rather than one, classified by the number of joints involved in the first 6 months and by systemic and serological features. Arthritis in a growing child has consequences that adult disease does not: inflammation increases blood flow to the nearby growth plate, so an affected knee can grow faster and produce a leg length difference, while long-standing disease can close growth plates early.

Oligoarticular JIA, involving four or fewer joints, is the most common form, about half of cases. It typically affects girls aged about 1 to 5 years and involves large joints such as a knee or ankle, often with little pain. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) is positive in most. Its most dangerous feature is chronic anterior uveitis, which is silent: unlike the acute painful uveitis of AS, it causes no pain, redness, or photophobia, and a young child does not report gradual blurring. Undetected, it causes posterior synechiae, band keratopathy, cataract, glaucoma, and permanent vision loss. ANA positivity and young age at onset identify the children at highest risk, and because there are no symptoms, only slit-lamp examination detects it.

Systemic JIA, about 10% of cases, behaves as an autoinflammatory disease driven by the innate cytokines IL-1 and IL-6 rather than by autoantibodies, so ANA and RF are usually negative. It presents with a quotidian fever that spikes once or twice daily to 39°C (102.2°F) or higher and returns to normal or below between spikes, for at least 2 weeks. An evanescent salmon-pink macular rash appears with the fever spikes. Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis are common, and arthritis may appear only later. Laboratory tests show leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, anemia, and very high ferritin and inflammatory markers. Its serious complication is macrophage activation syndrome, in which uncontrolled macrophage activation causes falling blood counts, a falling ESR (as fibrinogen is consumed), and extreme ferritin.

blocks.text: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease results when calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals form in articular cartilage. Chondrocytes generate extracellular inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi), partly through the ANKH transporter and the enzyme ENPP1, and PPi combines with calcium in the cartilage matrix. Crystals form when the product of calcium and PPi concentrations rises, or when the enzymes that degrade PPi are inhibited. Age is the main risk, so CPPD is common after 60; when it appears in a younger person, a metabolic cause should be sought.

blocks.text: When crystals shed from cartilage into the joint space, they activate the NLRP3 inflammasome and IL-1 beta release in the same way as urate, so acute pseudogout looks like gout: a hot, swollen, painful joint, sometimes with fever. The knee is most often involved, followed by the wrist, and attacks commonly follow surgery, trauma, or acute medical illness. The calcified cartilage itself appears on radiographs as chondrocalcinosis, a thin line of calcification within the hyaline cartilage or the fibrocartilage of the knee menisci, the triangular fibrocartilage of the wrist, and the pubic symphysis. CPPD can also produce a chronic degenerative arthropathy in joints that osteoarthritis usually spares, such as the second and third MCP joints in hemochromatosis.

CPPD crystals are rhomboid or short rods and weakly positively birefringent, appearing blue when their long axis is parallel to the slow axis of the compensator. Urate crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent, appearing yellow in the same orientation.

blocks.text: Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is inflammation followed by fibrosis of the glenohumeral joint capsule, especially the rotator interval, coracohumeral ligament, and inferior axillary recess. Early synovial inflammation gives way to proliferation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts that lay down dense collagen, a process similar to Dupuytren contracture. The capsule thickens, contracts, and adheres, and joint volume falls sharply. It most often affects people aged 40 to 60, women more than men, and runs through a painful freezing phase, a stiff frozen phase, and a slow thawing phase over about 1 to 3 years.

Diabetes is the strongest risk factor, raising the risk several fold and producing more severe and bilateral disease. Chronic hyperglycemia forms advanced glycation end products that cross-link collagen and stiffen connective tissue, the same mechanism behind limited joint mobility in the hand. Hypothyroidism and prolonged immobilization after injury or surgery are other associations.

Because the problem is a shrunken capsule, motion is limited mechanically in every direction, and both active and passive range of motion are lost, with external rotation lost first and most. This finding separates it from rotator cuff disease: in a cuff tear, the patient cannot actively lift the arm, but the examiner can move it passively through a full range, and in impingement the range is full with a painful arc. Radiographs are normal, which helps exclude glenohumeral osteoarthritis.

A ganglion cyst is the most common soft tissue mass of the hand and wrist. It arises from myxoid degeneration of connective tissue next to a joint capsule or tendon sheath, where fibroblasts produce hyaluronic acid rich mucin that collects in pools that coalesce. The wall is compressed collagen with no synovial or epithelial lining, so it is a pseudocyst, often connected to the joint by a stalk that may act as a one-way valve. About two thirds arise on the dorsal wrist over the scapholunate ligament, with others on the volar wrist or the flexor tendon sheaths of the fingers. The mass is firm, smooth, transilluminates, and varies in size with activity; most are painless, though some compress nearby nerves.

integration.text: Most disorders in this chapter are best organized by the tissue under attack. The spondyloarthropathies (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and enthesitis-related JIA) target the enthesis through HLA-B27 associated IL-23 and IL-17 inflammation, so they share sacroiliitis, dactylitis, anterior uveitis, a negative RF, and new bone formation. RA targets synovium and destroys bone. Gout and pseudogout are innate immune responses to crystals through the NLRP3 inflammasome, so their attacks look alike and are separated by chemistry: purine metabolism and renal urate handling for gout, cartilage pyrophosphate and mineral metabolism for CPPD. In the myopathies, the target is capillaries in dermatomyositis and the muscle fiber itself in polymyositis, while PMR inflames periarticular structures and leaves muscle intact.

Two laboratory values carry much of the reasoning, with limits. CK measures fiber necrosis, not weakness, so it is normal in PMR, steroid myopathy, and fibromyalgia for different reasons, and can be normal in early or skin-limited dermatomyositis. ESR measures systemic inflammation, not its site, and is high in PMR, GCA, and active spondyloarthropathy but normal in fibromyalgia and overuse lesions. Tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis, de Quervain disease, ganglion cysts, and adhesive capsulitis are local degenerative or fibrotic processes, so they produce no systemic signs, but their anatomy (which tendon, which arch, which capsule) predicts the examination findings.

summary: Ankylosing spondylitis is HLA-B27 associated enthesitis and sacroiliitis in young men; repair ossifies entheses into syndesmophytes and a bamboo spine, and back pain improves with exercise.

AS complications follow the tissue involved: painful anterior uveitis, aortic root fibrosis with aortic regurgitation and heart block, chest wall restriction, and unstable fractures of a fused osteoporotic spine.
Superficial bursae (prepatellar, olecranon) suffer pressure and skin breaks and become septic, mostly from Staphylococcus aureus; deep bursae (subacromial, trochanteric) are inflamed by overuse.
Fibromyalgia is central sensitization: widespread pain for at least 3 months with fatigue and unrefreshing sleep, mostly in women, with normal ESR, CRP, CK, and strength.

Hyperuricemia arises mostly from renal underexcretion; overproduction comes from tumor lysis, HGPRT deficiency, and glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency; xanthine oxidase makes urate from hypoxanthine and xanthine.
Gout crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent, trigger IL-1 beta through NLRP3, and cause podagra, tophi, punched-out erosions, and radiolucent uric acid stones.

Dermatomyositis is complement-mediated capillary injury with perifascicular atrophy, skin signs, and cancer risk; polymyositis is endomysial CD8 T cell attack; anti-Jo-1 marks interstitial lung disease.

High CK with weakness means myositis; normal CK with weakness suggests steroid myopathy (type II fiber atrophy); normal CK and strength with high ESR suggests PMR, which travels with giant cell arteritis.

Reactive arthritis is sterile, HLA-B27 associated arthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis 1 to 4 weeks after Chlamydia or enteric infection; psoriatic arthritis involves DIP joints, nails, and dactylitis with pencil-in-cup deformity.

Pseudogout crystals are rhomboid and weakly positive with chondrocalcinosis; adhesive capsulitis loses active and passive motion; oligoarticular JIA hides silent uveitis and systemic JIA spikes daily fevers.
